You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The test BrentSolverTest.testBadEndpoints() expects an IllegalArgumentException to be thrown in certain invalid scenarios such as when the interval is specified backwards (min > max) or when the function values at the endpoints do not bracket a root. These cases are handled by the solve(UnivariateRealFunction f, double min, double max) method, which verifies the interval and that the function values at min and max bracket a root, throwing an exception if not.

The current bug report points out that the solve method with the signature solve(UnivariateRealFunction f, double min, double max, double initial) does not throw an IllegalArgumentException when the values of the function at the three points min, max, and the initial guess all have the same sign, though the Javadoc claims it should.

Looking at the implementation of the solve(f, min, max, initial) method, it first calls verifySequence(min, initial, max) (which likely validates the ordering of these points, but does not check signs). It then evaluates f at min, max, and the initial point and checks if any of these values is close enough to zero. It then checks if the pairs (min, initial) or (initial, max) bracket the root by verifying if the product of function values at those points is negative, and in those cases calls the private solve method on the reduced interval. However, if neither pair brackets a root (i.e., function values at all three points have the same sign), it proceeds to call solve(f, min, yMin, max, yMax, initial, yInitial) without throwing the expected IllegalArgumentException in that case.

This reveals the source of the bug: The code does not explicitly check and throw an exception if the function values at min, max, and initial all have the same sign. It only checks for bracketing using pairs (min, initial) or (initial, max). If none of those bracket a root, instead of throwing an exception, it proceeds to run the Brent algorithm on an interval that does not bracket a root, which is against the specification and documentation.

In contrast, the two-argument solve method properly throws an IllegalArgumentException when the function values at min and max do not bracket a root, as observed in the test and in the code snippet for solve(f, min, max).

Hence, the failure of the test and the reported bug occur because the solve method with the initial guess parameter does not enforce the bracketing requirement when the initial guess is provided, leading to improper state and violating the documented behavior of throwing IllegalArgumentException.

Recent bug reports retrieved are unrelated to this issue and do not provide additional useful information.

Summary:
- The bug is located in BrentSolver.solve(f, min, max, initial).
- The method does not check if f(min), f(max), and f(initial) have different signs to ensure bracketing.
- It should throw IllegalArgumentException if values at all three points share the same sign.
- The absence of this check leads to the bug described in the current report and test failure.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
